subtype: Approach: saying sorry for his part and asking to play again [Action]
passage:
"Lalit. Wait."
Lalit stopped by the water cooler but didn't turn round.
"About yesterday. When you slipped in the mud at PT." Bhupen swallowed. "I laughed. I'm sorry. I didn't mean to hurt you. It was a stupid laugh."
"Everyone laughed after you did."
"I know. That's why I'm saying it first."
Lalit turned. His ears were red. "You laughed so loud."
"I know. Sorry. Really."
A long pause. The recess bell rang.
"...Football?" Bhupen held up the ball he'd brought from home. "You can be striker."
Lalit looked at the ball, then at him. "I'm always striker."
"Okay. Always striker."
Lalit almost smiled. "Come on, then."

qa.q: Where did Lalit stop?
qa.a: By the water cooler.

qa.q: What does Bhupen's swallowing suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He felt nervous and guilty about laughing, but determined to say sorry first.

qa.q: What could Bhupen do if Lalit had said no to football?
qa.a: Give Lalit time and keep being kind, maybe sitting together at lunch; the sorry still matters even if the game comes later.

qa.q: How does Lalit experience the apology?
qa.a: Lalit is still hurt, with red ears and 'You laughed so loud', but the sorry and the offer let him almost smile and join the game 🙂

grounding: Shows a boy going to his friend the next day, saying sorry for laughing and that he meant no hurt, then asking to play football at recess.

subtype: Approach: saying sorry for his part and asking to play again [Action]
passage: The morning after I laughed at Tenzin, I felt like I'd swallowed a stone. He'd tripped over his own shoelace in the assembly line and I'd laughed the loudest. His face had gone red and he hadn't looked at me since. At breakfast Aai said, 'Omkar beta, you're very quiet.' I told her. She only asked, 'So what will you do?' At school I walked straight to Tenzin before I could chicken out. 'I'm sorry I laughed yesterday. I didn't mean to hurt you.' He looked at his shoes. 'It was embarrassing.' 'I know. Want to play football at recess? I'll pass to you.' He shrugged, but at recess he was on my team.

qa.q: What did Tenzin trip over?
qa.a: He tripped over his own shoelace in the assembly line.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel the morning after laughing?
qa.a: Omkar felt guilty and heavy, as if he'd swallowed a stone, and was very quiet at breakfast.

qa.q: Why did Omkar's apology work?
qa.a: He said sorry for his exact part, the laugh, said he didn't mean to hurt, and then offered something to do together, football at recess.

qa.q: How did the laugh feel to Tenzin?
qa.a: Tenzin found it embarrassing and avoided looking at Omkar, though he still joined the team at recess.

grounding: Illustrates a boy apologising the next day for laughing, saying he did not mean to hurt, and inviting his friend to play football at recess.

subtype: Approach: waiting for the other friend to say sorry first [Pitfall]
passage: In their Class 7 classroom, Nandini's and Jomon's desks were still side by side, but for four days they had not said a word. It had started over a group project Jomon handed in with only his name on it. Nandini was sure it was all his fault. He should say sorry first, she decided. Jomon, it seemed, had decided the same. By Tuesday the girls at the back had started sitting with Nandini, and the boys stopped passing her the ball at games. On Thursday Nandini ate lunch alone under the stairs, looking at Jomon eating alone by the tap. Neither of them moved.

qa.q: How many days had Nandini and Jomon not spoken?
qa.a: Four days.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling as she ate alone under the stairs?
qa.a: She seemed lonely and stubborn, sure it was Jomon's fault yet missing him.

qa.q: What would you change first for Nandini?
qa.a: Speak first without taking all the blame, like 'I was upset about the project; can we talk?'; waiting for Jomon kept them both alone.

qa.q: How does the fight look from Jomon's side?
qa.a: Jomon is also waiting and eating alone by the tap, so he seems just as lonely and stuck.

grounding: Shows a girl sure a fight was her friend's fault and refusing to speak first, while days pass, both feel lonely and classmates take sides.

subtype: Approach: waiting for the other friend to say sorry first [Pitfall]
passage: I sit behind Sabina and Sunaina in class, so I've watched the whole silent war. It began last Monday, something about a secret Sunaina told someone. Since then, not one word. Sabina says, loudly enough for us to hear, 'She has to say sorry first. It was all her.' Sunaina says nothing, but she doesn't say sorry either. By Wednesday the class had split: half of us sat with Sabina at lunch, half with Sunaina. On Friday I saw Sabina sitting on the swing alone, not swinging, watching Sunaina across the ground. I don't know what either of them was thinking. But nobody looked happy.

qa.q: What does Sabina say loudly?
qa.a: 'She has to say sorry first. It was all her.'

qa.q: What might Sabina have been feeling on the swing on Friday?
qa.a: Sitting alone, not swinging, and watching Sunaina suggests she felt lonely and sad, even while holding to her rule.

qa.q: What could break the silence between Sabina and Sunaina?
qa.a: One of them saying something small first, or asking a teacher to help them talk; waiting for the other has only split the class.

qa.q: What has the fight been like for the rest of the class?
qa.a: The class has had to pick sides at lunch, so the others are caught up in a fight that isn't theirs.

grounding: Illustrates two girls each waiting for the other to apologise first, while days pass, both look lonely and the class splits into sides.

subtype: Approach: telling other classmates his side of the story [Pitfall]
passage: Tejas, you want to tell the whole class what Mohan did? Listen to your Tushar Kaka first. When I was eleven, my best friend Gopal and I fought over a game of marbles. I was sure he cheated. So I told the boys in my lane. Then the boys at school. By the third day, the story was that Gopal had stolen my marbles and hit me. I had said neither! Gopal heard it from someone else, and he was so angry he wouldn't even walk down the same road as me. I wanted to be proved right; instead I lost him for a whole year. We only made up at his sister's wedding.

qa.q: What had the story become by the third day?
qa.a: That Gopal had stolen the marbles and hit him.

qa.q: Why did young Tushar tell everyone his side?
qa.a: He felt angry and sure Gopal had cheated, and wanted to be proved right.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have kept the friendship?
qa.a: Talking to Gopal directly about the marbles instead of telling the lane and the school; spreading the story made it grow and harder to mend.

qa.q: How did Gopal experience the story spreading?
qa.a: Gopal heard an exaggerated version from someone else and was so angry and hurt that he avoided even walking the same road for a year.

grounding: Shows a boy telling others his side of a quarrel to be proved right, and the story growing until his friend is angrier and the rift lasts.

subtype: Approach: telling other classmates his side of the story [Pitfall]
passage: The school picnic bus was packed and noisy, and Hemant was still angry. Sharmila, the quiz captain, had picked Ravi instead of him for the inter-school team. 'She's so unfair,' he told the boy beside him. By the next stop, three rows knew. By the time they reached the dam, the story had grown: Sharmila picked only her friends; Sharmila said Hemant was stupid. Sharmila had said nothing like that. At lunch she marched up to him, eyes wet and furious. 'You told everyone I called you stupid?' Hemant opened his mouth. He hadn't said that exactly. But he had started it. She sat at the far end of the bus all the way home.

qa.q: Where was the picnic bus going?
qa.a: To the dam.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel when Sharmila confronted him?
qa.a: He was stuck for words and probably ashamed, knowing he hadn't said it exactly but had started the story.

qa.q: What could Hemant have done instead of telling the bus?
qa.a: Ask Sharmila privately why she chose Ravi, or talk to the quiz teacher; spreading his side only made the story grow and her angrier.

qa.q: What was the picnic like for Sharmila?
qa.a: Sharmila heard she'd said things she never said, so she felt hurt and furious, and sat far away all the way home.

grounding: Illustrates a boy telling classmates his friend was unfair, and the story spreading and growing until she is angrier and harder to make up with.

subtype: Approach: writing a small note if talking feels too hard [Action]
passage:
Thursday night
Yesterday I shouted at Zubin in the art room because he spilled water on my painting. I've felt sick in my stomach about it ever since. Today I tried three times to go and say sorry, but my mouth closed every time. I'm like that; the other girls say I'm too quiet, and my voice just disappears. So in maths I tore a page from the back of my notebook and wrote: 'Zubin, I'm sorry I yelled. It was only paint. Friends again? Hansa.' I folded it small and slipped it into his desk before lunch. After lunch there was a paper boat on my desk. Inside: 'Yes. Sorry about the water 🙂'

qa.q: What did Hansa find on her desk after lunch?
qa.a: A paper boat, with 'Yes. Sorry about the water' inside.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel about shouting at Zubin?
qa.a: Hansa felt guilty and anxious about it, sick in the stomach ever since.

qa.q: Why was a note a good choice for Hansa?
qa.a: Her voice disappears when she's nervous, so writing let her say sorry clearly and gave Zubin time to reply.

qa.q: How might Zubin have felt finding the note?
qa.a: Zubin seemed relieved and ready to make up, replying 'Yes' and saying sorry for the water too.

grounding: Shows a shy girl who cannot say sorry aloud writing a short note and putting it in her friend's desk, giving the friend time to reply.

subtype: Approach: writing a small note if talking feels too hard [Action]
passage: At the village school Tanuja hardly spoke above a whisper, except on Monday, when she had shouted at Nirmala for stepping on her skipping rope. Everyone had turned to look. Now, two days later, Tanuja couldn't find her voice at all. After the prayer bell she tore the corner off her notebook and wrote slowly: 'I am sorry for shouting. Will you skip with me again?' She folded it into a tiny square and pushed it into Nirmala's desk while the others were filling water. Nirmala found it during the Hindi lesson, read it twice, and didn't look up. Tanuja's heart thumped. At the end of school, Nirmala was waiting by the gate, holding the rope.

qa.q: What had Nirmala stepped on?
qa.a: Tanuja's skipping rope.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja's heart thump during the Hindi lesson?
qa.a: She felt nervous and anxious, not knowing how Nirmala would react, because Nirmala didn't look up.

qa.q: What made the note work well here?
qa.a: It let shy Tanuja say sorry without speaking, and gave Nirmala time to read it twice and decide how to answer.

qa.q: How might Nirmala have felt reading the note twice?
qa.a: Nirmala probably felt touched and took time to think, then answered by waiting at the gate with the rope.

grounding: Illustrates a shy girl writing a sorry note and slipping it into her friend's desk, which gives the friend time to feel and respond.

subtype: Approach: asking a teacher for help to talk it out [Revision]
passage:
Wednesday
Tried to make up with Devika today. Didn't work. I said, 'Can we talk?' and she said, 'About how you told everyone my marks?' and I said, 'I didn't tell everyone!' and then we were both shouting again, right in the corridor. I went home and cried. Tonight I thought hard. Every time we try, it turns into the same fight. We can't fix this by ourselves. So tomorrow I'm going to ask Mrs Fernandes to sit with us.
Thursday (adding this)
She did! In the empty staff room. She said, 'Devika first, then Ayesha. No interrupting, girls.' It felt strange, but for the first time I actually heard what Devika was upset about.

qa.q: Where did Mrs Fernandes sit with them?
qa.a: In the empty staff room.

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel after the first attempt?
qa.a: Ayesha felt upset and hopeless, crying at home after it turned into shouting again.

qa.q: What made the second try work better than the first?
qa.a: Mrs Fernandes set turns with no interrupting, so each girl could be heard instead of both shouting.

qa.q: How might Devika have experienced the talk in the staff room?
qa.a: Speaking first without being interrupted, Devika could finally explain what upset her, which may have helped her feel heard.

grounding: Shows a girl whose first try to make up ends in shouting, who sees they can't fix it alone and asks the class teacher to let each speak in turn.

subtype: Approach: asking a teacher for help to talk it out [Revision]
passage: Neelam and Sarita had shared a bench at the panchayat school since Class 1. Now they weren't speaking, all because of a torn library book each blamed on the other. On Monday Neelam tried: she walked up to Sarita at the hand pump and said, 'Let's forget it.' Sarita said, 'You mean forget that you tore it?' Within a minute they were shouting, and a crowd gathered. That evening Neelam sat on the roof thinking. We're only going round and round. We need someone in the middle. On Tuesday she went to Kamla Bahenji, the class teacher. At lunch Bahenji sat with both of them under the peepal tree and said, 'Sarita speaks, then Neelam. Nobody cuts in.'

qa.q: What did each girl blame on the other?
qa.a: A torn library book.

qa.q: What was Neelam thinking and feeling on the roof?
qa.a: She felt frustrated that they were 'only going round and round', and saw that they needed someone in the middle.

qa.q: Why did asking Kamla Bahenji help where Neelam's first try failed?
qa.a: The teacher gave each girl a turn with no cutting in, so the talk couldn't turn into shouting at the hand pump again.

qa.q: How might Sarita see sitting under the peepal tree with the teacher?
qa.a: Sarita gets to speak first without Neelam cutting in, so she may feel respected and more willing to listen.

grounding: Illustrates a girl whose first attempt to make up ends in shouting, realising they need help, and asking the class teacher to let each speak in turn.

subtype: Approach: offering a fair fix like taking turns [Action]
passage: Every lunch break in the schoolyard in Valencia, the football game started with the same fight: Pablo wanted to be captain, and so did Diego. On Monday they shoved each other and the whole break was lost to arguing. On Tuesday Mei, who kept the ball, said, "Can't you just take turns?" The two boys looked at each other. "Me today, you tomorrow," Diego offered. "And then swap every day after that," said Pablo. They shook on it. Mei wrote the days on a card and stuck it on the ball bag. On Wednesday, when Diego started to argue out of habit, Pablo just pointed at the card: WED, PABLO. Diego laughed, dropped his water bottle by the wall, and joined Pablo's team.

qa.q: Who kept the ball?
qa.a: Mei kept the ball.

qa.q: How did Diego seem to feel when Pablo pointed at the card?
qa.a: He laughed, so he seemed at ease with it, knowing his own turn was fair and coming.

qa.q: What could the boys do if more players want to be captain?
qa.a: Add them to Mei's card in turn; writing the days down is what stopped the same quarrel starting again.

qa.q: How did the lunch-break fights look to Mei?
qa.a: Mei watched a whole break lost to arguing, so Mei was probably fed up, and glad the card fixed it.

grounding: Shows two boys ending a fight over who is captain by agreeing to swap captains each day, which is fair and stops the quarrel recurring.

subtype: Approach: offering a fair fix like taking turns [Action]
passage: At the Sunday cricket camp in the Ludhiana stadium, Gurpreet and Amandeep had spent twenty minutes arguing over who would captain the practice match. Coach Baljit blew his whistle. "No match until you two sort it out." They glared at each other by the boundary rope. Then Amandeep said, "Okay. What if you're captain today, I'm captain next Sunday, and we keep swapping?" Gurpreet thought. "And whoever isn't captain opens the batting." "Deal." They wrote it in the back of the coach's register: G, A, G, A. The match started ten minutes later. The next Sunday, nobody argued at all.

qa.q: Where did they write the plan?
qa.a: In the back of the coach's register: G, A, G, A.

qa.q: What might Gurpreet have felt when Amandeep suggested swapping?
qa.a: He probably felt relieved and fairly treated, and added his own idea about opening the batting.

qa.q: Why is swapping a better fix than one boy giving in?
qa.a: It treats both fairly every week, so neither feels he lost, and the same quarrel doesn't come back next Sunday.

qa.q: How does Coach Baljit see the problem?
qa.a: Coach Baljit sees twenty minutes lost to arguing and insists they sort it out themselves before any match.

grounding: Illustrates two boys settling a quarrel over captaincy by agreeing to alternate captains, a fair fix that stops the fight from returning.

subtype: Approach: pretending nothing happened and acting normal [Thinking]
passage: Rain kept everyone indoors at recess, which made it harder: Anand and Pema were stuck in the same classroom after yesterday's fight over the carrom striker. Anand thought it through. If I talk about it, we'll just fight again. Better to act normal. He unwrapped his mother's chakli, the kind Pema loved, and held out the box. "Want some?" Pema paused, then took one. They munched, talking about the rain. It seemed to work. But when Anand said, "Carrom after school?", Pema's face closed. "You called me a cheater yesterday," Pema said quietly. "In front of everyone." Anand's hand froze on the box. The chakli hadn't fixed that.

qa.q: What did Anand offer Pema?
qa.a: His mother's chakli, the kind Pema loved.

qa.q: Why did Anand decide to act normal?
qa.a: He was worried that talking about it would start another fight, and hoped acting normal would make things feel okay again.

qa.q: What could Anand add to his approach now?
qa.a: A sorry for calling Pema a cheater in front of everyone; sharing food eased the mood, but the hurt needed to be spoken about.

qa.q: How did the snack look from Pema's side?
qa.a: Pema accepted the chakli and chatted, but was still hurt about being called a cheater, so the snack felt like skipping over it.

grounding: Shows a boy offering a snack as if there had been no fight, which eases things briefly but leaves his friend's hurt unspoken.

subtype: Approach: pretending nothing happened and acting normal [Thinking]
passage: In the lane behind their Kolkata building, Gautam and Lavanya had squabbled that morning over who batted first. It was over in a minute, but they'd gone home without saying bye. At five, Gautam stood at Lavanya's door with two jhalmuri cones from the corner cart. He'd thought about it on the stairs. It was only batting. If I make a big speech, it'll be weird. Just act normal. "Jhalmuri?" he said. Lavanya grinned and grabbed one. "I'm batting first today, though." "Fine." Walking down, Gautam thought: that worked because she wasn't really hurt. Last month, when I laughed at her drawing, jhalmuri wouldn't have been enough.

qa.q: What did Gautam bring to Lavanya's door?
qa.a: Two jhalmuri cones from the corner cart.

qa.q: Why did Gautam decide to act normal instead of apologising?
qa.a: He felt the batting squabble was small and was worried a big speech would feel awkward.

qa.q: When would Gautam's snack approach not be enough?
qa.a: When the friend is still really hurt, as when he laughed at Lavanya's drawing; then he'd need to talk about it and say sorry.

qa.q: How did Lavanya seem to feel about the jhalmuri?
qa.a: Lavanya grinned and took it, teasing that she'd bat first, so she seemed happy and not holding on to the squabble.

grounding: Illustrates a boy acting as if nothing happened and sharing a snack, which works for a small squabble but would not mend a deeper hurt.

subtype: Approach: copying rules from a game they already know [Thinking]
passage: On the terrace of their Jaipur building, five children were bored of the same old games. "Let's invent a new one," Parul said. Vidya groaned. "We'll spend all evening making rules." Parul thought out loud. "What if we don't start from nothing? Kabaddi has two sides and a line in the middle. Tag has catching. So a raider crosses the line, tags someone and gets back, but instead of holding breath, the raider has to hop." Vidya's eyes lit up. "And if you're tagged, you join the other side, like in tag." They chalked a line down the middle of the terrace. Within ten minutes, the first raider was hopping across.

qa.q: What did they chalk on the terrace?
qa.a: A line down the middle.

qa.q: How did Vidya feel when Parul explained the idea?
qa.a: Vidya's eyes lit up, so Vidya went from bored and doubtful to excited about the game.

qa.q: What could the group do if their borrowed rules don't fit well?
qa.a: Play a round and change one rule at a time; borrowing from kabaddi and tag gave them a working start instead of a blank page.

qa.q: How might the other children on the terrace see the new game?
qa.a: They get a game that feels familiar yet new, so they can start playing within minutes instead of arguing over rules.

grounding: Shows children designing a terrace game by borrowing rules from kabaddi and tag, giving them a working start.

subtype: Approach: copying rules from a game they already know [Thinking]
passage:
"I'm bored of kabaddi."
"I'm bored of tag."
"So let's make a new game," said Sangeeta.
"From scratch? That'll take forever," Anand said.
"Not scratch. Take bits. Kabaddi: two teams, a middle line, one raider goes over."
"And from tag?"
"The raider tags, and whoever's tagged has to freeze. Like freeze tag."
"How do they unfreeze?"
"A teammate crawls under their legs."
Anand counted the terrace tiles. "Middle line here. Teams of four."
"And the raider has to keep saying 'chaka-chak' instead of 'kabaddi'."
Everyone laughed. "Chaka-chak! Okay. First raid, Anand!"

qa.q: What does the raider have to keep saying?
qa.a: 'Chaka-chak', instead of 'kabaddi'.

qa.q: How did Anand feel about making a new game at first?
qa.a: Anand felt doubtful and a bit impatient, thinking it would take forever from scratch.

qa.q: Which part of Sangeeta's thinking made the game quick to start?
qa.a: Taking pieces from games everyone already knew, kabaddi's teams and raider and tag's freezing, so nobody had to learn everything new.

qa.q: How do the others seem to feel about 'chaka-chak'?
qa.a: Everyone laughs, so they seem amused and excited to start.

grounding: Illustrates children building a new terrace game from pieces of kabaddi and tag, so they have a working start without inventing everything.

subtype: Approach: deciding the goal and how someone wins first [Thinking]
passage: Kamal, your new game has no end, so everyone just runs till they fight. Let your Kalyani Paati tell you something. When I was ten, in our street in Thanjavur, we made up games every evening, and they always fell apart. One day I said, 'Wait. How does anyone win?' Nobody knew. So we decided that first: five flags, made from old saree bits, hidden at each end. First team to bring home all five wins. Only then did we make the other rules: you carry one flag at a time, and you can be caught only on the other side. That game lasted all summer, and we even taught it to my cousins from Madurai.

qa.q: What were the flags made from?
qa.a: Old saree bits.

qa.q: How might young Kalyani have felt when the games kept falling apart?
qa.a: She was likely frustrated and puzzled, which led her to ask how anyone wins.

qa.q: What was the key choice in the story, and why did it help?
qa.a: Deciding the goal first, five flags, so every other rule could be built to serve that end.

qa.q: How did the other children in the street experience the new game?
qa.a: They got a game with a clear finish that lasted all summer, good enough to teach to the cousins from Madurai.

grounding: Shows a girl insisting a game needs an end, her group settling on five flags to win, and then building the movement rules around it.

subtype: Approach: deciding the goal and how someone wins first [Thinking]
passage: Recess was only twenty minutes, and half the ground was taken by the older kids' cricket, so Sarita's group had a strip of grass by the wall. Tushar was already explaining rules: "You run here, then you jump there, then..." "Stop," Sarita said. "How does someone win? Games have to finish somehow, or we'll just run around till the bell." Everyone looked at her. "Five flags," she said. "Our handkerchiefs, five each side. First team to steal all five wins." Then the rest came quickly: you can take only one at a time; if you're tagged on their side, you freeze. When the bell rang, Tushar's team had four, and they were already planning a rematch.

qa.q: How long was recess?
qa.a: Only twenty minutes.

qa.q: Why did Sarita say 'Stop' to Tushar?
qa.a: She was impatient with rules that had no end and worried they'd just run around till the bell.

qa.q: What does Sarita's approach suggest for making any game?
qa.a: Decide how someone wins first, then build the other rules around that goal, so the game makes sense quickly.

qa.q: How might Tushar see Sarita cutting in?
qa.a: Tushar was mid-explanation, but his team got four flags and wanted a rematch, so he seems to have enjoyed the game she shaped.

grounding: Illustrates a girl saying a game needs an end, the group choosing five flags as the goal, and building the other rules around it.

subtype: Approach: playing a quick trial round to test it [Action]
passage: At the community centre's summer camp, Binita's group had invented a relay game, but they couldn't agree on half the rules. "Let's just play five minutes and see," Binita said. Rose didi, the helper, set her phone timer. Round one: Thomas won. Round two: Thomas again. Round three: Thomas, grinning, not even out of breath. The timer beeped. Everyone flopped down. "It's not a game," someone said. "It's just Thomas running." Binita thought. "What if the last five steps are hops? On one foot?" They tried it. Thomas wobbled; a smaller girl, Chinmayi, hopped steadily past him. Everyone cheered, including Thomas.

qa.q: How many rounds did Thomas win in the trial?
qa.a: Three rounds.

qa.q: How did the others feel after Thomas won three times?
qa.a: They flopped down and said 'It's just Thomas running', so they felt bored and fed up.

qa.q: Why was a five-minute trial a good idea?
qa.a: It showed the problem, the same fast runner winning, before they spent time fixing every rule; one change, hopping, then fixed it.

qa.q: How did Thomas seem to feel about the hopping rule?
qa.a: Thomas wobbled and lost to Chinmayi but still cheered, so he seemed to enjoy the fairer game.

grounding: Shows children testing their game for five minutes, seeing the same fast runner always wins, and adding a hop rule for the last steps.

subtype: Approach: playing a quick trial round to test it [Action]
passage: I watched from our balcony as Simran and the building kids tried their new game in the courtyard. They hadn't finished the rules, but Simran said, 'Five minutes, just try.' It was a race to the water tank and back with a ball. Rafiq won the first round. Then the second. Then the third, by miles. The little ones started drifting off towards the swings. Simran called everyone back and said something I couldn't hear, waving her arms. Next round, I saw them all hopping the last few steps to the tank, on one foot, falling over, laughing. Rafiq came fourth. I don't know if he minded. He was laughing too.

qa.q: Where did the race go?
qa.a: To the water tank and back, with a ball.

qa.q: What might Simran have been feeling when the little ones drifted off?
qa.a: She may have felt worried that the game was failing, which is why she called everyone back and changed a rule.

qa.q: What could the group test next?
qa.a: Another short round with the hop rule, watching whether different children win; quick trials show which rule needs fixing.

qa.q: How did Rafiq seem to experience the new rule?
qa.a: Rafiq came fourth but was laughing too, so he seemed to enjoy the game even without winning.

grounding: Illustrates children playing a quick trial of their game, noticing one fast runner always wins, and adding a hopping rule for the final steps.
